title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 133
paragraphs: When they meet one another in the roads, you can tell by this whether those who meet are of equal rank: for instead of greeting by words, they kiss one another on the mouth; but if one is a little inferior to the other, they kiss one another on the cheeks; and if one is of much less noble rank, he falls down before him and does him obeisance. They honor most, after themselves, those nations which dwell nearest to them, and next those which dwell next nearest, and so they go on giving honor in proportion to distance. They hold in least honor those who dwell furthest from themselves, esteeming themselves to be by far the best of all the human race in every respect, and thinking that others possess merit according to this proportion, so that those who dwell furthest from themselves are the worst. Under the supremacy of the Medes, the various nations also used to govern one another according to the same rule the Persians observe in giving honor: the Medes governed the whole, and in particular those who dwelt nearest to themselves; these, in turn, ruled over those who bordered upon them; and those again over the nations next to them. For the race proceeded thus, always from government by themselves to government through others.
